newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Reform needed to revive Bosnian industry-experts.
newsitem.headline: Reform needed to revive Bosnian industry-experts.

text.p: Bosnia's industry boasts a number of attractive industrial sectors for investors, but foreign experts say the country needs to open its gates to free-market reforms before it can spark interest.

The forestry and wood-products industry, metal industries, construction materials and components sectors, electric products and mineral processing are singled out by analysts as Bosnia's most promising assets.

"Any of the industries that we've listed should be magnets for capital. It would be hard at this point for any investment not to be productively used (in these areas)," David King, of the U.S. Agency for International Development, told Reuters.
Industry in Bosnia suffered $20 to $40 billion worth of damage during its 3-1/2 year war, the World Bank estimated, but King said that a number of sectors remain attractive potential investments.
Experts like King say the most difficult task facing Bosnia is not repairing war damage but abandoning a pre-war, Yugoslav socialist legacy of centrally-planned economics.
The country badly needs commercial legislation that clarifies company ownership, corporate governance and financial markets to allow Bosnian companies to attract foreign capital.

"And the biggest issue is the privatisation. Both sides (Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic) are dragging their feet on privatisation," another U.S. AID analyst, Demos Menegakis, said.

Coming out of a 43-month war, Bosnia is slowly reviving its battered economy with a pledged $1.8 billion injection from foreign donors' money in 1996. Donors will be asked to pledge another $1.4 billion for reconstruction in 1997.
"We'll start to see in 1997 (a) little bit of opening up to the international private investor community," King said.
But he said a high government priority should be the removal of obstacles to creating the right conditions for private investors.
Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation government has sent draft legislation on privatisation to the parliament, but it has yet to adopt the law.

"I expect the set of laws on privatisation to be endorsed at the next federation parliament session at the end of January or beginning of February," said Ivo Krizanovic, a government official in the ministry of energy, mining and industry.

The international community delivered a stern warning to the Bosnian government this week that the next donor fund-raising conference set for March in Brussels would not make sense unless the country carried out economic reforms.
They are needed to allow for a transition from donors providing emergency relief to using funds for the building of a sustainable economy, experts said.
"You cannot be a charity case forever. Whoever is smart enough to realise that and do something about it, now is the time," Menegakis said.
King and Menegakis work in the "Bosnia Business Assistance Centre" funded by U.S. AID, which tries to help companies reorganise and lure foreign capital.
"The single missing capability in the whole of Bosnian industry is marketing. Bosnia has the capability to manufacture good products but it needs to focus on marketing," Menegakis said.
